title: Vitamin C Won't Stop Your Cold
hook: Fifty years after Linus Pauling popularized megadoses, the verdict is in: vitamin C doesn't stop most people catching colds. Taken regularly, it may shorten severe symptoms slightly.
key_points: The megadose idea traces to Nobel laureate Linus Pauling, who popularized it over 50 years ago.
Larger studies since then found vitamin C does not prevent most people from catching a cold.
Taking it regularly may make severe symptoms slightly shorter or milder — a small effect.
Starting it once you already feel sick is not where the modest benefit was found.
A useful case study in how one prominent advocate can outlast the evidence.
content_html: If you keep vitamin C on hand to head off colds, the evidence isn't on your side. The belief goes back more than 50 years to Nobel laureate Linus Pauling, who championed huge doses. The larger studies that followed found that vitamin C does not prevent most people from catching a cold.
extra_html: There is one small survivor from all that research: people who take vitamin C regularly may find severe symptoms slightly shorter or milder. Note the word regularly — that's different from starting a supplement the moment your throat feels scratchy. It's a modest payoff, and a good reminder of how a well-known advocate's confidence can keep an idea alive far longer than the data supports. For an actual cold, rest, fluids, and time still do the heavy lifting. Reported by ScienceDaily.

related.title: Caring for a Cold or Flu at Home
related.hook: Most colds and flu run their course on their own. Good home care is about comfort and rest — and knowing the handful of red flags that mean it's time to get checked.

related.title: A $70 Billion Industry With Thin Evidence
related.hook: Supplements are one of the fastest-growing corners of health spending. For most of what's on the shelf, there's little evidence it does what the label implies.

related.title: Cold, Flu, or COVID?
related.hook: They share a lot of symptoms, but colds, flu, and COVID-19 differ in how fast they hit and how hard — and telling them apart can change what you do next.

flashcards.prompt: What do larger studies say vitamin C does for colds?

choices.text: It doesn't prevent most colds, but regular use may slightly shorten severe symptoms
It prevents most colds if the dose is high enough
It has no effect on colds whatsoever

flashcards.explanation_html: Prevention doesn't hold up for most people. The surviving effect is small: taken regularly, vitamin C may make severe symptoms somewhat shorter or milder.

flashcards.prompt: Where did the 'megadose vitamin C beats colds' belief come from?
flashcards.back_html: Linus Pauling, a Nobel Prize winner, popularized it more than 50 years ago. His prominence carried the idea long past what the later, larger studies supported.

flashcards.prompt: Regular use vs. starting at the first sniffle — which showed the modest benefit?
flashcards.back_html: Regular ongoing use. The small effect on severity was found in people already taking it, not in those who reach for it after symptoms begin.
